strengths: The central hypothesis — that data quality, not model scale, is the bottleneck for neural invariant synthesis — is clearly articulated and directly tested through a well-designed three-way ablation (V0 raw, V1 normalized, V2 simplified+verified) across three model scales, showing monotone improvements that support the claim.

The pipeline is methodologically sound: unlike prior fine-tuning work on raw verifier output, every LLM-rewritten candidate is re-validated by a formal verifier for both inductiveness (V1) and sufficiency (V2), so training data correctness is guaranteed by construction (Proposition 4.3). This is a rigorous and appropriate use of symbolic tooling to supervise neural data curation.

The formalization of 'good' training invariants (non-degeneracy, correctness, usefulness, compactness) and the quality grading function Q provide a reusable, precise framework for future work on data curation for verification tasks.

The ablation results are convincing and interpretable: V0 training actually hurts validation rate (99.2%→81.3% for 4B), V1 restores syntax, and V2 yields the large semantic gains (correctness 22.8%→44.4%, speedup 11.1%→24.7%), cleanly isolating each pipeline stage's contribution.

The VBP/VBS portfolio-based metric is a sensible reframing of evaluation for generate-and-verify systems that run in parallel with a symbolic baseline, and reporting both VBP and VBP_E2E (with/without inference latency) is transparent.

Good reproducibility posture: code, datasets, and fine-tuned models are released; full SFT hyperparameters, sampling parameters, UAutomizer configuration, and hardware details are provided in appendices.

Results are reported as mean ± std over three runs, and the paper honestly discusses nuance (e.g., the 0.6B correctness parity with improved practical utility) and the remaining open problem of baseline timeouts.
weaknesses: Evaluation scope is narrow: all experiments use a single verifier (UAutomizer) on a single benchmark suite (InvBench/SV-COMP), and only the Hard split (n=123). The authors acknowledge additional verifiers as future work, but generalization of the claims beyond this setting is untested.

There is a potential train/evaluation overlap concern: training programs come from the InvBench training set and evaluation instances are derived from InvBench programs (via loop expansion). The paper does not explicitly certify that the 123 hard evaluation instances are disjoint from the 7,283 curated training samples' underlying programs, which is essential to rule out leakage-driven gains.

The headline claim that the 4B model 'approaches' GPT-5.2 is overstated: GPT-5.2 achieves 72.4% correctness and 37.1% speedup versus 44.4% and 24.7% for Qwen3-4B-V2. The claim holds only for VBP/VBP_E2E timing (165.5s vs 163.4s), which should be stated more precisely.

With n=123 instances, 3 runs, and no statistical significance testing, some reported gaps (e.g., the 'Solved' column differences of 2–3 instances, or 0.6B base vs. V2 at 27.9% vs 28.5%) may not be statistically meaningful; the paper does not address significance.

The dataset size is modest (7,283 samples) and the curation pipeline itself relies on a frontier LLM (Kimi K2 Thinking) with N=4 candidates per verbose invariant; the compute/cost of curation is not reported, which matters for assessing the practicality of the approach.

Stripping integral type casts can break soundness under overflow (acknowledged), meaning the 'normalization' stage is not uniformly semantics-preserving in practice despite Proposition 4.1; correctness is only restored downstream by re-verification, which is fine for training but slightly undercuts the framing of the two stages.

The comparison to prior fine-tuning work (Wei et al., 2025 / InvBench) is effectively the only external baseline; no comparison against other data-centric strategies (e.g., synthetic program generation, rejection-sampled LLM data, RLHF-style verifier feedback) is provided, limiting our understanding of why this curation approach is the right one.
Contributions 1 and 3 of the framing (Propositions 4.1/4.3) are technically trivial; the real contribution is empirical, so the formal dressing adds limited depth.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: solver-generated invariants are noisy training targets, and the paper operationalizes 'data quality' via four concrete properties (non-degeneracy, correctness, usefulness, compactness) rather than treating curation as a vague notion.

The pipeline is sound by construction: every LLM-simplified candidate is re-verified for correctness (V1) and sufficiency (V2) before entering the training set, and Propositions 4.1/4.3 state the guarantees explicitly, including an honest acknowledgment that stripping type casts can break soundness.

The ablation study (Table 4) is informative and supports the central claim: raw invariants (V0) degrade validation and can hurt correctness at small scale, normalization (V1) fixes syntax but not semantics, and the simplified/verified data (V2) yields the largest gains (e.g., speedup 12.7% -> 24.7% for Qwen3-4B).

The proposed VBP/VBS portfolio metric is a reasonable reframing: since the LLM runs in parallel with the symbolic baseline, failures are zero-risk, and reporting both VBP and VBP_E2E partially addresses the latency concern.
Reproducibility is treated seriously: full prompts, grading and simplification algorithms, hyperparameters, verifier configuration, and stated releases of code, models, and data.
weaknesses: Evaluation scope is narrow and possibly biased: results are reported exclusively on 123 'Hard' instances derived from a single verifier (UAutomizer), with the Easy split entirely discarded. The paper's contribution is a data-curation recipe, yet there is no evidence it transfers to other verifiers (Eldarica, etc.), other benchmark suites, or the full instance distribution; this is acknowledged only as future work.

Potential train/evaluation contamination is not addressed. Both the training programs and the evaluation instances come from the InvBench authors' SV-COMP-derived releases, and the paper never states that training programs are disjoint from evaluation instances. Given that the headline gains come from fine-tuning on this distribution, this omission is a material soundness gap.

The headline comparisons to frontier models are overstated. 'Matches GPT-OSS-120B and approaches GPT-5.2' rests on VBP differences within overlapping error bars (165.5±3.2 vs 165.8±5.6 vs 155.6±3.0), while the fine-tuned 4B model's correctness rate (44.4%) remains far below GPT-5.2 (72.4%) and GPT-OSS-120B (58.0%). The abstract's 'doubles the invariant correctness and speedup rates of base models' also does not hold for the 0.6B model, whose correctness is flat (28.5% -> 27.9%).

The VBP gains, while real, are modest in absolute terms (roughly 12-20 seconds on a mean baseline of 193s, i.e., ~6-11%), and the decision-procedure framing assumes the two sub-queries are always simpler than the original; no analysis is given of cases where invariant-annotated verification is slower or the decomposition changes the outcome semantics in edge cases.

Ablations do not isolate the confound between LLM-rewriting and simply having shorter invariants: V2 differs from V1 both in provenance (Kimi K2 rewrites) and in brevity, and there is no control (e.g., heuristic minimization without an LLM, or an SFT baseline on trivially-truncated invariants) to attribute the gain specifically to 'semantic simplification'.

Some claims are thin on evidence: Contribution 1 ('directly bootstrapping ... can sometimes even hurt performance') is supported by one model's validity drop in the ablation, and the paper's hypothesis that compactness facilitates learning/generalization is asserted but never measured directly (e.g., no correlation between training-invariant length and downstream performance).

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: multiple grammatical errors ('various for techniques', 'to curation training data', 'this work help make', 'VBPE2E mteric'), and Figure 1/Table 1 semantics around FALSE outcomes and timeout handling of the 20 timed-out baseline instances are not fully spelled out.

strengths: The methodology is formally grounded: the pipeline's soundness is carefully argued (Propositions 4.1 and 4.3), and every LLM-generated training invariant is validated by a sound verification oracle, which is a rigorous and appropriate use of symbolic tools to guarantee data quality.

The ablation study (Table 4) is well designed and convincingly isolates the contribution of each pipeline stage: raw invariants (V0) can even hurt validation rates, normalization (V1) restores syntax but not semantics, and simplification (V2) drives most of the gain (e.g., correctness 22.8% -> 44.4% and speedup 11.1% -> 24.7% for Qwen3-4B). This directly supports the central 'data quality, not model scale' thesis.

The critique of sequential speedup metrics and the proposed portfolio-based VBP/VBS metric reflect genuine deployment realities (LLM as a parallel, zero-risk augmentation), and the paper transparently reports both VBP and VBP_E2E including model latency.

Reproducibility is strong: full codebase and models/datasets are released, prompts, hyperparameters (Tables 5-6), sampling parameters, verifier configuration, and hardware details are all provided, and the decision procedure is precisely specified.

The limitations discussion is honest: cast-stripping may break soundness (mitigated by re-verification), baseline timeouts remain largely unsolved, the 0.6B result shows a nuanced correctness-vs-utility trade-off, and reliance on a single backend verifier (UAutomizer) is acknowledged as future work.
weaknesses: Potential train/evaluation contamination is not adequately addressed. Both the training programs (released by InvBench authors) and the evaluation instances (also derived from SV-COMP via InvBench) come from the same source, yet the paper never explicitly states that the training programs and the 362 evaluation instances are disjoint. Given the fine-tuned models achieve a suspiciously perfect 100.0% syntactic validity and large gains specifically on hard instances, this overlap must be clarified or the headline results cannot be fully trusted.

The claim that the 4B model 'approaches the state-of-the-art GPT-5.2' is overstated. VBP is comparable (165.5s vs 155.6s), but GPT-5.2 substantially outperforms on correctness (72.4% vs 44.4%) and speedup rate (37.1% vs 24.7%), and solves more baseline timeouts (2.67 vs 2.33 on average). VBP compresses these differences because it is dominated by the shared baseline verifier time.

The contribution is relatively incremental: the pipeline is a combination of known components (AST rewriting, LLM-based simplification, verifier filtering), closely extending Wei et al. (2025), who already fine-tuned on UAutomizer invariants. The novelty lies mainly in the curation insight and the quality grading, which is valuable but modest.

The evaluation is narrow: only 123 hard instances from one benchmark family, one verifier as both teacher and baseline, and three stochastic runs with sometimes large variance (e.g., Rvalid std of ±7.8 for Qwen3-8B base). No statistical significance testing is reported, and generalization to other verifiers or program domains is untested.

The claimed 'doubling' of correctness and speedup rates does not hold at all scales: for Qwen3-0.6B, correctness is essentially unchanged (28.5% -> 27.9%), so the abstract's framing is somewhat selective.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('the and only if ERROR is unreachable', 'mteric', 'curation training data', 'this work help make'), and the claimed VBP improvement 'up to 14.2%' is a relative number against the verifier-only baseline that readers may over-interpret; absolute reductions are 12-20 seconds.

strengths: The paper clearly formalizes the problem (Hoare logic, verification queries, correctness vs. sufficiency checks, §3) and defines concrete, measurable properties of 'high-quality' training invariants (non-degeneracy, correctness, usefulness, compactness), which is a useful conceptual contribution beyond the pipeline itself.

Soundness of the data curation pipeline is well handled: every transformation that may not preserve semantics (cast stripping, LLM rewriting) is followed by formal verifier validation (Algorithm 1, Proposition 4.3), so the central claim that curated data preserves provable correctness is supported by construction.

Thorough and transparent empirical evaluation: a V0→V1→V2 ablation across three model families (Table 4), easy/hard splits (Tables 3, 5), three runs with standard deviations, a post-hoc timeout sweep (Appendix E.2), and benchmark characterization. The evaluation adopts the established InvBench framework of Wei et al. (2025), enabling direct comparison.

Good reproducibility: full prompts (Appendix B), training hyperparameters (Tables 6-7), sampling settings (Table 8), verifier version/configuration (Table 9), hardware, and public code are provided. Dataset pipeline yield statistics are reported in detail (Appendix D).
Honest limitations section: the authors themselves acknowledge dependence on UAutomizer as sole invariant source, risk of inheriting solver bias, and lack of iterative/RL refinements.
weaknesses: Moderate novelty: the core recipe—AST normalization plus LLM-driven rewriting with verifier-based rejection filtering—is a fairly standard data-curation pattern; the main delta over Wei et al. (2025) is data quality engineering rather than a new method or new understanding of why it works. No analysis (e.g., which simplification goals drive gains, or what the model actually learns) is provided to substantiate the 'pedagogical value' hypothesis beyond aggregate metrics.

Contribution 1 ('fine-tuning on raw solver invariants does not reliably improve performance and can even degrade it') is only partially supported by the paper's own ablation: Table 4 shows V0 fine-tuning substantially improves Rcorrect for Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B (e.g., Llama 14.9%→31.2%); the degradation is mainly in syntactic validity (Rvalid). The framing somewhat overstates the failure of the raw-data baseline.

Headline claims about matching frontier models deserve more caution. Qwen3-14B-V2 'matches GPT-5.2' only on VBP_E2E (162.9±8.1 vs. 163.4±3.0 s), a difference far inside one standard deviation, while its correctness rate (43.4%) is far below GPT-5.2's (72.4%). Several cross-model VBP differences (e.g., 165.5 vs. 166.5 s) are within noise; no statistical significance tests are reported. Similarly, Qwen3-0.6B-V2 slightly decreases correctness relative to base (27.9% vs. 28.5%), which is glossed over in the main narrative.

Potential circularity: the same verifier (UAutomizer) is used both as the source of training invariants and as the oracle whose speedup defines data quality (grade G) and evaluation success. Time-based filtering (tv < tb) with wall-clock times also raises concerns about measurement noise; it is unclear how many runs back t1/t2 (only tb uses a 3-run median).

The evaluation is confined to one benchmark suite (InvBench/SV-COMP-derived, 123 hard instances from 72 programs), and the practical benefit assumes ideal portfolio deployment (VBP excludes inference latency; VBP_E2E only adds it for sufficient instances). Generalization to other verifiers or out-of-distribution programs is untested.

The compactness hypothesis ('succinct form facilitates learning and generalization') is asserted but never isolated; compactness is entangled with usefulness filtering (grade ≥ 2) in the V2 dataset, so the specific role of each design choice in the pipeline is not disentangled.

strengths: The core idea is sound and well-executed: training targets are formally validated (correctness and sufficiency checks against the verifier), so the 'provable quality guarantees' claim is supported, and Propositions 4.1/4.3 correctly scope what is and is not guaranteed (the LLM rewriting step is explicitly not semantics-preserving, with soundness recovered via verification).

The ablation design (V0 raw → V1 AST-normalized → V2 full pipeline) is informative and directly supports the paper's central claim that data quality, not scale, is the bottleneck; the V0 validity degradation (e.g., Qwen3-4B 99.2% → 81.3%) is a genuinely useful negative finding for the community.

Evaluation is unusually careful for this area: three runs with std. reported, a timeout sweep, per-instance VBS/VBP metrics with an explicit decision procedure (Table 1), and a clear separation of correctness from speedup (the Qwen3-0.6B decoupling analysis).

Reproducibility is strong: full prompts (Appendix B), algorithms, SFT/LoRA hyperparameters, sampling settings, UAutomizer version and configuration, hardware, and dataset yield statistics are all provided, with code released.
The limitations section is honest about the single-verifier dependence, solver-bias inheritance, and lack of reasoning/RL components rather than obscuring them.
weaknesses: Originality is modest. The pipeline is essentially: strip casts/tautologies, then prompt a large LLM (Kimi K2 Thinking) with simplification guidelines and rejection-filter candidates via the verifier. This is a standard distillation-with-verification recipe; the four 'transformation goals' are prompt heuristics, and no analysis is given of which mechanism (compactness, diversity, format) drives the gains — compactness facilitating learning is only 'hypothesized'.

The headline claims of matching frontier models are overstated. 'Matching GPT-5.2' rests on VBP_E2E of 162.9±8.1 vs 163.4±3.0 — well within noise — while correctness is 43.4% vs 72.4% and R_valid is 96.5% vs 94.0%. Similarly, the 4B 'matching GPT-OSS-120B' claim (165.7 vs 167.6 s) carries the same issue. The VBP metric is also a portfolio metric that assumes parallel execution of the baseline; the primary metrics exclude inference latency, which flatters the SLM comparisons until the E2E addendum.

Absolute end-to-end impact is modest: VBP improves from 193 s to ~163–169 s (~12–16%), and only ~18–25% of hard instances actually achieve a speedup. Timeouts remain largely unsolved (2–4 of 20). The paper is candid about this, but it tempers the significance of the 'accelerates verification' framing.

Potential train/test distribution proximity is not addressed: training programs come from Wei et al. (2025) and evaluation uses InvBench, also derived from SV-COMP; the paper does not discuss contamination or distribution overlap between fine-tuning programs and the hard split.

The dataset is small (7,284 samples) and derived solely from UAutomizer, and the pipeline's dependence on an external frontier LLM for simplification is itself a cost and bias the paper does not quantify (no analysis of simplification-stage failure modes or yield sensitivity to the choice of simplifier).

Qwen3-0.6B shows essentially no correctness gain (28.5% → 27.9%), suggesting the approach depends on a minimum model capacity, yet the abstract and conclusion generalize the result to 'SLMs' without this caveat.

The negative claim in Contribution 1 ('fine-tuning on solver outputs does not reliably improve performance and can even degrade it') is only partially supported: V0 fine-tuning actually improves R_correct on most models; what degrades is syntactic validity, which is a different (and weaker) statement.

strengths: The paper formalizes what constitutes a 'good' training invariant (non-degeneracy, correctness, usefulness, compactness) and grounds the curation pipeline in this definition, which is a clear conceptual contribution over prior work that simply used raw solver output.

Soundness of the pipeline is handled carefully: every LLM-driven rewrite is re-verified with the formal verifier (Proposition 4.3), so no unverifiable data can leak into training. This is the right way to use an LLM as a rewriting engine in a verification setting.

The ablation study (V0 raw → V1 AST-normalized → V2 full pipeline, Table 4) is well designed and run consistently across three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1, Mistral), and the pattern (V0 can even degrade syntactic validity, V1 partially recovers, V2 gives the largest gains) is convincing evidence that data curation, not just fine-tuning, is the operative factor.

Evaluation is thorough: hard/easy splits, three runs with std, a post-hoc timeout sweep, benchmark characterization, full hyperparameters, prompts, verifier configuration, and hardware details. Reproducibility appears good, with public code and released artifacts from the prior work it builds on.

The metrics (VBS/VBP/VBP_E2E) are carefully defined, and the paper is commendably transparent that correctness and speedup are decoupled (e.g., the Qwen3-0.6B case where correctness is flat but speedup improves).
Limitations are honestly discussed: single backend verifier (UAutomizer), inheritance of solver biases, no reasoning traces or verifier-feedback loop.
weaknesses: The headline claim that a 4B model 'matches' GPT-OSS-120B and a 14B model 'matches' GPT-5.2 on end-to-end verification time rests on differences of ~1–2 seconds (e.g., 162.9±8.1 vs 163.4±3.0; 165.7±3.2 vs 167.6±5.7) that are well within the reported standard deviations. No statistical significance testing is performed despite three runs, so these equivalence claims are not statistically supported. The substantial correctness gap (43–45% vs 58–72% for the frontier models) is downplayed in the abstract and conclusion.

The absolute improvements on the hard split are modest in wall-clock terms (VBP drops from ~193s baseline to ~165–169s, i.e., roughly 12–16%), and the VBP metric by construction caps gains at the baseline solver time (min(tv, tb)), which structurally favors the LLM portfolio approach; the framing 'surpasses a 20x larger model' overstates what the numbers show.

The V2 training set is generated by a very strong teacher (Kimi K2 Thinking), so part of the improvement may reflect distillation of a frontier model's reasoning rather than 'data curation' per se; the paper does not disentangle the contribution of the LLM rewriting stage's capability from the curation/verification machinery (a cheaper-teacher control is absent).

The evaluation is confined to InvBench (362 instances, 123 hard), derived from SV-COMP and released by Wei et al., which is also the source of training programs. Potential distributional overlap between solver-verified training programs and the evaluation set is not discussed, and the benchmark's small size makes the per-run variance in 'Solved' counts (0–4 of 20 timeouts) hard to interpret.

Contribution originality is moderate: the pipeline combines known ingredients (AST normalization, LLM rewriting, verifier filtering, SFT), and the central finding—training data quality matters—is plausible but established here through engineering rather than a new method or a new understanding that generalizes beyond this benchmark; generality of WONDA to other verifiers or domains is asserted only as future work.

Some pipeline details are heuristic and under-justified: the verbosity threshold (η = 20 chars), the grade-2 cutoff, and the decision to retain non-speedup candidates; no sensitivity analysis for these hyperparameters is provided. The G = 2 tier (correct and sufficient but no speedup) makes up ~62% of the training data, which sits somewhat awkwardly with the paper's emphasis on 'usefulness' as a defining property.

The claim of 'provable quality guarantees' is weaker than it sounds: normalization is provably semantics-preserving (Prop 4.1), but the LLM rewriting stage is only sound because of the external verifier check—appropriate, but the framing slightly oversells the formal guarantee.
